solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Start off with exploit that is to restrict tax

parts.note: an exploit is a deed, an act
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, 'that is'
value added tax, the British sales tax

explanation.surface: Someone planning a new venture means to begin by using a loophole to cap their tax bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exploit' looks like a verb, but it is the noun, a daring deed; VAT is the British equivalent of a sales tax.
explanation.definitionFit: To activate something is to start it off, set it going.

clue.text: Duke's odd — one has stretched skin

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for Duke
rum is British slang for odd or strange

explanation.surface: A peculiar aristocrat, apparently marked out by his tight, stretched skin.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is read as 'is': Duke is odd, D + RUM. 'Rum' meaning strange is old-fashioned British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: every drum is a frame with a skin pulled taut across it.

clue.text: Tricky period in which to work before end of day

indicators.note: the working period comes before the last letter in the answer

parts.note: a shift is a working period

indicators.note: the end of 'day' is its last letter only

explanation.surface: A worker grumbles about an awkward stint that has to be fitted in before the day ends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tricky' looks like it describes the period, but it is the definition standing alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Shifty and tricky both describe someone crafty and not to be trusted.

clue.text: B&B is near sprawling city

indicators.note: the letters sprawl out of their order

explanation.surface: An advert for a bed and breakfast boasts it is close to a big spreading city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sprawling city' reads as one phrase, but 'sprawling' is the anagram indicator acting on the words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Brisbane is the capital of Queensland, Australia.

clue.text: Cleric in Siberia distributed church books

indicators.note: the cleric goes in the rearranged Siberia
the letters of Siberia are distributed into a new order

parts.note: Rev, short for Reverend, a clergyman

explanation.surface: A missionary priest in Siberia hands out religious books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Distributed' in the surface is the priest handing books out; in the wordplay it scrambles Siberia.
explanation.definitionFit: A breviary is a book of the daily prayers and offices of the Church.

clue.text: Look — a delicate batting stroke!

definitions.meaning: a quick, brief look, the verb or the noun
a cricket shot that deflects the ball finely off the bat

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a glance is a shot that deflects the ball off the face of the bat, fine to the leg side.
explanation.definitionFit: A glance is a quick look, and also that deft cricket stroke.

clue.text: My hesitation about central heating after second day it isn't needed!

parts.note: s is the abbreviation for second
'Cor!' is a British exclamation of surprise, like 'My!'
the standard abbreviation, as in estate agents' ads

explanation.surface: Someone dithering about switching the heating on is told that, by the second day, it won't be needed.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on 'central heating' in the wordplay: 'it' is the heating, which nobody needs on a very hot day.
explanation.definitionFit: A scorcher is a very hot day, one when no heating is needed.

clue.text: Model again about to join company on stage

indicators.note: the word for about is joined to the company

parts.note: the cast is a play's company of actors

explanation.surface: A model is poised to join a theatre company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model' looks like a person, but here it is a verb: to shape.
explanation.definitionFit: To recast is to model or shape something again, as metal is recast.

clue.text: Artist and count meeting only very occasionally

parts.note: to count on someone is to rely on them

explanation.surface: A painter and an aristocrat who hardly ever see each other.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Count' wants to be a nobleman (EARL); it is the verb, as in 'count on'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something done only very occasionally is done seldom.

clue.text: Tree by front of mansion is well-rooted

indicators.note: the letter stands by the tree, next to it
the front of mansion is its first letter

explanation.surface: A tree standing by the front of a grand house has put down deep roots.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all about roots, but 'well-rooted' is used figuratively: solidly fixed.
explanation.definitionFit: Something firm is well-rooted, solidly fixed in place.

clue.text: Maintaining dignity, protecting a mug?

explanation.surface: Someone hangs on to their dignity while guarding a cup.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is the answer taken literally: saving a face, where 'mug' is slang for face rather than a cup.
explanation.definitionFit: A face-saving move is one that keeps your dignity intact.

clue.text: Festive occasion with a couple of unknowns –- lots of stars too

indicators.note: the festive occasion comes with the unknowns after it

parts.note: a gala is a festive occasion
x and y are the usual unknowns in algebra

explanation.surface: A gala night with a few nobodies on the guest list, and plenty of celebrities as well.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's stars are celebrities at the party; the definition means stars in the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: the Milky Way and its kind are huge systems holding billions of stars.

clue.text: Permits will be distributed at house, sir

indicators.note: the letters will be dealt out into a new order

explanation.surface: A butler tells his master that the permits will be handed out at the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Permits' is a noun in the surface but a verb in the definition, as in 'she permits it'.
explanation.definitionFit: To authorise is to permit; 'authorises' matches 'permits' as a verb.

clue.text: In a storm this may create wet areas

definitions.text: In a storm this may create wet areas

indicators.note: letters caught in a storm are tossed about

explanation.surface: In a storm, spray blown ashore leaves things soaked.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: 'wet areas' tossed in a storm spell the answer, and storm-driven seawater really does soak the coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Seawater whipped up by a storm floods and wets the land it reaches.

clue.text: Complete country, as it was, without Scripture

indicators.note: 'without' in its old sense of outside: the country sits outside the Scripture

parts.note: Eire, the former official name of Ireland

explanation.surface: A nation is made whole again, just as it used to be, but with religion left out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' wants to mean 'lacking', inviting a deletion; here it has its old sense of outside. Eire was Ireland's official name in English until 1949.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: complete and entire both mean whole, with nothing missing.

clue.text: Member of Communist organisation roughing up nameless undergrad

indicators.note: the remaining letters are knocked about

parts.note: n is short for name; it is removed, leaving UDERGRAD

explanation.surface: A party militant beats up an anonymous student.
explanation.walkthrough: The Red Guards were the student militias of Mao's Cultural Revolution in 1960s China, which fits the surface's thuggery.
explanation.definitionFit: A Red Guard was a member of those young Communist paramilitary units.

clue.text: University tower that somehow enthrals one

indicators.note: to enthral is to hold captive, so the rearranged letters hold the one inside
the letters of 'tower that' end up somehow, in some new order

explanation.surface: A university's tower somehow captivates a visitor.
explanation.walkthrough: Heriot-Watt is a university in Edinburgh; 'tower' looks like part of the definition but is anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Heriot-Watt University is named after George Heriot and James Watt.

clue.text: Source of pleasure is English paper

explanation.surface: Someone declares that reading an English newspaper is a real pleasure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'English paper' reads as a newspaper, but the E comes off 'English' and 'paper' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A paper can be a scholarly essay, and a treatise is a formal written study.

clue.text: Hell, sound of clock! Gets you agitated

indicators.note: the answer is what the two words sound like said together

parts.note: 'Heck!' is a mild 'Hell!', and a clock goes tick

explanation.surface: Someone cursing at a loudly ticking clock finds it winds them up.
explanation.walkthrough: Heck is the polite form of 'hell' as an oath; said quickly, 'heck-tick' is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Hectic means frantic, agitated with activity.

clue.text: A cool den specially made for pet

indicators.note: the letters are made into something new

explanation.surface: A snug kennel built specially for a family pet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pet' is the animal in the surface, but the definition is the verb: to kiss and cuddle.
explanation.definitionFit: To canoodle is to pet, kiss and cuddle amorously.

clue.text: Plant to reduce to nothing around start of autumn

indicators.note: the verb goes around the letter

parts.note: to annul is to cancel, make void

indicators.note: the start of autumn is its first letter

explanation.surface: A gardener cuts a plant right back as autumn begins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' looks like a verb, 'to plant'; it is the noun, and 'to' links it to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: An annual is a plant that lives for a single year.

clue.text: Speed of something like chicken crossing a street

indicators.note: the hen crosses the street by spanning it, one half each side

parts.note: a hen is one kind of chicken

explanation.surface: The old joke about why the chicken crossed the road, here asking how fast it went.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Speed' reads as a noun in the surface but is the verb in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean to hurry, and both can be used with or without an object.

clue.text: Hushing up corporal punishment?

definitions.meaning: keeping something quiet or out of sight
a thrashing, as given at school in the old days

explanation.walkthrough: A hiding is a beating, from 'hide' meaning to thrash someone's skin.
explanation.definitionFit: Hiding is concealing or hushing up; a hiding is also a thrashing.

clue.text: Awfully quaint, a Fifties youth is seen as behind the times

indicators.note: the letters are put in an awful mess

parts.note: a Ted, or Teddy boy, was a 1950s British youth in Edwardian-style dress

explanation.surface: A 1950s youngster looks terribly quaint to modern eyes.
explanation.walkthrough: Teddy boys were British 1950s youths known for drape jackets and quiffs, shortened to Teds.
explanation.definitionFit: Antiquated means old-fashioned, behind the times.

clue.text: See 17
Put on report of conflict

indicators.note: a report is something heard, so we want the word's sound

parts.note: conflict is war; in a British accent, with no R sounded, it rhymes with 'door'

explanation.surface: A dispatch from a war zone was being broadcast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Report' suggests journalism, but here it just means sound; 'war' and 'wore' rhyme in non-rhotic British speech.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Put on' as in clothes: yesterday she put on, or wore, a coat.

clue.text: Rush wildly in vehicle, always in poetic style

parts.note: e'er, the poetic contraction of ever

explanation.surface: A reckless driver always tears about, as if in a poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In vehicle' looks like a container instruction, but nothing goes inside: 'in' only links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain verb sense: a runaway cart careers down a hill, rushing along out of control.

clue.text: Assembly wanting advance? Con, not pro!

indicators.note: CON goes in where PRO is not, replacing it

parts.note: names the letters PRO at the front of the advance that are taken out

explanation.surface: A political assembly that wants to move forward, with the opposition shouting down the proposers.
explanation.walkthrough: Pro and con are the familiar opposites for and against; swap one for the other at the start of PROGRESS.
explanation.definitionFit: A congress is a formal assembly, like the US legislature.
